course.title: Personal Finance & FinTech
course.shortDescription: Master the money fundamentals — compound interest, markets, financial statements, and diversification — then see how FinTech is rebuilding all of it in software.
course.longDescription:
This showcase course pairs the freeCodeCamp Fundamentals of Finance & Economics curriculum with original readings on financial technology. Video segments cover money basics, financial markets, business strategy, financial statements, capital budgeting, macroeconomics, and portfolio management — interleaved with scenario quizzes and a Python challenge where you compute compound interest yourself, the calculation behind every savings account and loan.

The final module connects the theory to the FinTech industry: digital payments, neobanks, robo-advisors, and the risks and regulation that come with money-as-software.
course.courseSummary: Time value of money and compound interest, financial markets and instruments, business strategy, the three financial statements, capital budgeting (NPV), macroeconomics (GDP, inflation, interest rates), ESG, portfolio diversification, alternative investments, and the FinTech landscape.

content.description: Key financial terms, why a dollar today beats a dollar tomorrow, and compound interest in action.
content.problemStatement: Key financial terms, why a dollar today beats a dollar tomorrow, and compound interest in action.

contentBlocks.content:
The most important formula in personal finance

A dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year — because today's dollar can be invested and grow. That single idea, the time value of money, underlies every savings account, loan, pension, and stock valuation. Its engine is compound interest:

A = P × (1 + r)ⁿ

where P is the starting amount (principal), r the annual rate, and n the number of years. The "compound" part means each year's interest itself earns interest — which is why $1,000 at 8% becomes not $1,800 after 10 years (simple interest) but $2,159.

  • Watch for: the Excel compound-interest case study — you will re-implement it in Python later
  • Watch for: inflation as compound interest working against you

content.description: Stocks, bonds, and the marketplaces where they trade — who participates and why.
content.problemStatement: Stocks, bonds, and the marketplaces where they trade — who participates and why.

contentBlocks.content:
Where capital meets ideas

Financial markets exist to move money from people who have it (savers, investors) to people who can use it (companies, governments). The two instruments to understand first:

  • Stocks (equity) — you own a slice of the company; unlimited upside, real downside, no promises
  • Bonds (debt) — you lend money for a fixed interest payment; capped upside, higher claim if things go wrong

Everything else — ETFs, mutual funds, derivatives — is packaging around these two. This segment tours the marketplaces themselves: exchanges, brokers, and the participants from pension funds to day traders.

  • Watch for: the risk/return trade-off — higher expected return always prices in higher risk

content.description: How companies compete and grow — the strategy concepts investors use to judge a business.
content.problemStatement: How companies compete and grow — the strategy concepts investors use to judge a business.

contentBlocks.content:
Numbers follow strategy

Before reading a company's financials, understand its strategy — the choices about where to compete and how to win. A durable competitive advantage (a "moat") is what lets a company earn above-average returns for years: brand, network effects, switching costs, or cost leadership. This segment introduces the strategic lenses analysts apply before they ever open a spreadsheet.

  • Watch for: differentiation vs. cost leadership as the two basic ways to win
  • Watch for: why growth without a moat gets competed away

content.description: Income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement — the three lenses on any business.
content.problemStatement: Income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement — the three lenses on any business.

contentBlocks.content:
Three statements, three questions

Every public company reports the same three statements, and each answers a different question:

  • Income statement — Is it profitable? Revenue minus expenses over a period → net income
  • Balance sheet — What does it own and owe? A snapshot obeying the iron equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
  • Cash flow statement — Where did the cash actually go? Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact

The classic trap this segment defuses: a company can report positive net income while running out of cash (customers haven't paid yet), or report losses while gushing cash. Reading all three together is the skill.

content.description: How businesses decide which projects deserve money — discounting future cash flows to today's value.
content.problemStatement: How businesses decide which projects deserve money — discounting future cash flows to today's value.

contentBlocks.content:
Time value of money, weaponized

Capital budgeting is compound interest run in reverse. A project promises cash flows in future years; to compare them fairly against the cost today, you discount each one back to present value and sum them up — the Net Present Value (NPV):

NPV = Σ  CFₙ / (1 + r)ⁿ  −  initial cost

Positive NPV → the project creates value; negative → it destroys value even if it "makes money" on paper. The discount rate r encodes both the time value of money and the project's risk.

  • Watch for: how a higher discount rate shrinks distant cash flows the most

content.description: GDP, inflation, and interest rates — the weather system every portfolio lives inside.
content.problemStatement: GDP, inflation, and interest rates — the weather system every portfolio lives inside.

contentBlocks.content:
The macro weather system

Three dials describe an economy's weather: GDP growth (is the economy expanding?), inflation (how fast are prices rising?), and interest rates (the price of money, steered by central banks). They interact constantly: when inflation runs hot, central banks raise rates; higher rates make borrowing expensive, cooling both the economy and — usually — stock prices.

  • Watch for: why bond prices fall when interest rates rise
  • Watch for: inflation silently taxing cash — the reason "safe" savings can lose purchasing power

content.title: Challenge: Compound Interest Calculator
content.question: Implement the calculation behind every savings account: A = P(1 + r)^n.
content.description:
Read three values from input (one per line):

P — principal (e.g. 1000)
r — annual rate as a percentage (e.g. 8 means 8%)
n — number of years (integer)

Print the final amount after n years of annual compounding, with two decimal places.

Example: P=1000, r=8, n=10 → 2158.92
content.problemStatement: Read principal, annual rate (percent), and years; print P × (1 + r/100)^n with two decimal places. Example: 1000, 8, 10 → 2158.92.

python.body:
principal = float(input())
rate = float(input())      # percentage, e.g. 8 means 8%
years = int(input())

# TODO: compute the compounded amount and print it
# with two decimal places, e.g. 2158.92
python.solution:
principal = float(input())
rate = float(input())
years = int(input())

amount = principal * (1 + rate / 100) ** years
print(f"{amount:.2f}")

content.description: Portfolio construction: why diversification is the only free lunch, plus ESG and alternative assets.
content.problemStatement: Portfolio construction: why diversification is the only free lunch, plus ESG and alternative assets.

contentBlocks.content:
"Diversification is the only free lunch"

Harry Markowitz's famous line captures the one reliable trick in investing: assets that don't move together cancel out some of each other's risk. A portfolio of ten uncorrelated bets is far less volatile than any single one, without sacrificing expected return. This closing segment covers diversification and portfolio management, plus two modern threads: ESG investing (weighing environmental, social, and governance factors) and alternative investments (real estate, commodities, private equity).

  • Watch for: correlation as the mathematical heart of diversification
  • Watch for: why "don't put all eggs in one basket" is about the relationships between baskets

content.description: Money as software: digital payments, neobanks, robo-advisors, BNPL, and the risks that come with them.
content.problemStatement: Money as software: digital payments, neobanks, robo-advisors, BNPL, and the risks that come with them.

contentBlocks.content:
Everything you just learned, rebuilt in software

FinTech is the re-implementation of financial services as software — taking the concepts from this course and making them instant, mobile, and cheap. The map of the territory:

  • Digital payments — UPI, mobile wallets, and real-time payment rails moving money in seconds instead of days; the largest FinTech category by volume
  • Neobanks — branchless, app-only banks with dramatically lower operating costs than incumbents
  • Robo-advisors — algorithms that build diversified portfolios automatically (the Markowitz math from the last unit, as a product)
  • Lending platforms & BNPL — credit decisions in seconds using alternative data; "buy now, pay later" is an installment loan with better UX
  • Blockchain & digital assets — decentralized ledgers removing intermediaries entirely, with volatility and regulatory uncertainty to match

The permanent trade-off

Every FinTech innovation trades convenience against new risk: instant payments enable instant fraud; algorithmic credit can encode bias (recall the AI course!); seamless BNPL makes over-borrowing frictionless. Regulation — KYC (know your customer), AML (anti-money-laundering), deposit insurance — exists to manage exactly these failure modes. A FinTech professional needs both halves: the finance to know what the product is, and the judgment to know how it breaks.

questions.title: Challenge: Savings Goal Planner
questions.question: Compute how many full years of compounding are needed to reach a savings goal.
questions.description:
Read three values from input (one per line):

P — starting amount
r — annual rate as a percentage
G — the goal amount

Print the smallest whole number of years of annual compounding after which the balance is at least G.

Example: P=1000, r=10, G=2000 → 8 (1000 × 1.1⁸ ≈ 2143.59 ≥ 2000, while year 7 gives ≈ 1948.72).

If the starting amount already meets the goal, print 0.
questions.problemStatement: Read principal, rate (percent), and goal; print the smallest integer n where P × (1 + r/100)^n ≥ G. Print 0 if P already meets the goal.

python.body:
principal = float(input())
rate = float(input())   # percentage
goal = float(input())

# TODO: count the years of compounding needed to reach the goal
# and print the count (print 0 if the goal is already met)
python.solution:
principal = float(input())
rate = float(input())
goal = float(input())

years = 0
balance = principal
while balance < goal:
    balance *= 1 + rate / 100
    years += 1
print(years)
